meta.note: Distilled by subagent from video transcripts (rolling, Aug 2026). Visibility-only: takes never move projections; adjustments require player_adjust.json with documented reasons. Prune takes AND facts older than ~3 weeks. Each take carries a separate 'mechanism' field — audit the mechanism independently of the conclusion before repeating it (see expert_methods.md -> Mechanism audit). direction 'contested' = the sources, or the FF hosts internally, disagree.

takes.why: Take him as your first or second WR at the 2-3 turn; if healthy for 14 games he clears 150 targets.
takes.mechanism: Led the NFL in target share as a rookie (170 targets in 15 games) and the only real target competition left (Wan'Dale Robinson, 140 targets each of the last two years) is gone, replaced by dusty vets and a third-round rookie; the ACL recovery scare that depressed his price in May/June has flipped — he has been running routes and cutting since late July and has now taken full team-drill reps 20 days before week 1.
takes.round_or_adp: 26th overall, 'second, usually the third round'; 'two three-turn'

takes.why: Slam-dunk pick as the TE10-13 in round 10-11 — he has finished better than TE13 in each of the last six seasons.
takes.mechanism: Co-led all TEs with 11 receiving TDs on a 30% red-zone target share that led the Eagles over A.J. Brown, DeVonta Smith and Saquon Barkley — and A.J. Brown is now in New England, while the rookie drafted to replace him (Eli Stowers, 2nd round) is reportedly struggling with NFL physicality and may not even be active weeks 1-2.

takes.why: Buy him at the 2-3 turn; 1,400-yard upside in New England.
takes.mechanism: Best QB of his career in Drake Maye (one vote from co-MVP, 29 attempts/game, 4th in deep attempts) plus a massive downgrade in target competition — from DeVonta Smith and Dallas Goedert to Romeo Doubs, Hunter Henry and Demario Douglas — and a reunion with Mike Vrabel, who oversaw his rookie 1,000-yard breakout.
takes.round_or_adp: 22nd overall; 'if he somehow falls to the 24th pick'

takes.why: Take him at the 3-4 turn as your second early RB — top-5 RB upside he has already shown in 2023.
takes.mechanism: 1,400 total yards and 36 catches last year on the worst passing offense in football (140 pass yards/game); the only thing missing was TDs (5), which he blames on the offense and QB room, not the back. Geno Smith is a clear QB upgrade, the Jets added zero backfield competition in free agency or the draft, they signed him to 3yr/$45M, and the groin injury depressing his price is really a 1-2 week issue being handled cautiously.
takes.round_or_adp: 34th overall, '34 turn' (3-4 turn); took him at 3.01 in the Flock League

takes.why: Fine to take at the end of round 6 — 1,000-yard, 8-TD upside with the price already baking in every scare.
takes.mechanism: The market is double- and triple-counting the same known risk (age 33, injury history, current quad tightness with 25 days to heal and no expectation he misses week 1); meanwhile he has no target competition in San Francisco — no Ricky Pearsall, a 33-year-old Kittle off a torn Achilles, a declining Deebo Samuel, Christian Kirk maybe not making the team — and he is the first true X receiver Brock Purdy has had since 2023 Brandon Aiyuk.
takes.round_or_adp: 68th overall, 'towards the end of the sixth round' (used to cost a fifth)

takes.why: Solid price in the fifth round even after the Stefon Diggs signing.
takes.mechanism: Last season is a mulligan (holdout, his own injuries, and only one or two games where he and Jayden Daniels were both healthy); in the only full year they played together he went 1,100 yards / 82 catches / 13 TDs, and even hurt last year he was 5th in first downs per route run, 13th in YPRR, zero drops, top-10 in yards per catch. Diggs works the slot while McLaurin wins intermediate-to-deep — they complement rather than overlap, and a better offense means more red-zone trips for both.
takes.round_or_adp: 'fifth round pick often at the four or five turn'

takes.why: The most slept-on Packer — unbelievable value in rounds 9-10 and a candidate to lead the team in receiving.
takes.mechanism: Romeo Doubs (the offense's Mr. Consistency) left for New England and Dontayvion Wicks was traded to Philadelphia, vacating a large share of Green Bay targets; Reed is WR1 on the Packers in fantasy points per target and passer rating when targeted since 2023, just got a 3yr/$50M extension, is 11 months removed from his collarbone injury and foot surgery, and Green Bay says it wants a faster pace and more 11 personnel.

takes.why: A great value at the 4-5 turn; another 150-target season is coming.
takes.mechanism: Before last year's injury he was averaging 19 PPR points and 9.6 targets a game on a 34% target share, second in the NFL only to Jaxon Smith-Njigba, and his down season came in the league's worst QB room. Geno Smith is an upgrade, and the feared target competition evaporated — rookie WR Omar Cooper is losing the slot job to UDFA Isaiah Williams and rookie TE Kenyon Sadiq missed OTAs, camp and preseason behind Mason Taylor — leaving Adonai Mitchell as the only downfield competition.
takes.round_or_adp: 47th overall, 'four or five turn', 'fourth to fifth round'

takes.why: Still a very good spot at WR36 in rounds 8-9 even after the Keenan Allen signing.
takes.mechanism: Michael Pittman Jr. is gone and Alec Pierce has missed all of camp with an unexplained issue (the Keenan Allen signing is itself the tell), so Downs plays outside in two-WR sets; Allen absorbs the shallow work, which per beat reporting should raise Downs' average depth of target, and Shane Steichen said on record his role 'is definitely going to improve this season.'
takes.round_or_adp: 89th overall, WR36, 'eighth or ninth round' (used to be 110-120)

takes.why: Maybe the best pick in all of fantasy — fine in round 4, a steal if he lasts to round 5; a 1,500-yard season is not crazy.
takes.mechanism: Last year's WR25 line was an offense problem, not a player problem — he ran only 23 routes a game (52nd in the NFL) because Miami's QB room could not sustain drives. Denver traded a first-round pick for him, Bo Nix led the NFL in pass attempts (612) and was third in deep attempts, and the only competition is a 30-year-old jump-ball Courtland Sutton; Sean Payton has compared his three-position versatility to Michael Thomas.
takes.round_or_adp: 38th overall, '34 turn'; 'especially if you can get him in round five, although now he goes in round four'

takes.why: Not fantasy relevant and not a real threat to Nabers' target share.
takes.mechanism: Good camp reports, but in the preseason game he was off the field in run-blocking situations; he may not play more than 50% of snaps, and under ~50% snaps a TE is never fantasy relevant.

takes.why: Do not draft him expecting to beat out Goedert this year.
takes.mechanism: Beat reporting (Zayn Dhani) says he is going through rookie-TE growing pains, struggling with NFL physicality, and may not even be active for weeks 1 and 2.

takes.why: A favorite of his all offseason in the sixth round, though he prefers Jayden Reed at the far cheaper price.
takes.mechanism: Watson is the big-play guy in the vacated Green Bay target pool, but he will not be the offense's 'Mr. Consistency' the way Reed can be.

takes.why: Worried about taking him in the second round.
takes.mechanism: The QB room he depends on looks sketchy in camp and preseason — Tua Tagovailoa and Michael Penix Jr. splitting work with neither seizing the job.
takes.round_or_adp: 'the second round of your fantasy drafts'

takes.why: No longer Denver's best receiver — Waddle is the clear number one 'with a bullet'.
takes.mechanism: This is a 30-year-old, mostly-downfield jump-ball receiver, not the Sutton of three years ago.

takes.why: Not a player they target in drafts, even though Jason expects him to be a top-24 PPR WR for the first month.
takes.mechanism: They do not target older PPR receivers in the super-late rounds — those picks should be spent on young rookie upside — and his production window shrinks as soon as Alec Pierce returns.

takes.why: Downgrade him — the Keenan Allen signing hits Downs harder than anyone on the Colts.
takes.mechanism: Jason wanted Downs on the field in two-WR sets; Allen has played 60/40 outside-to-inside in recent years and will take that role, Tyler Warren gets his, and Pierce returns to the outside, so the two-WR-set path Downs needed is gone. (Directly contradicts Sal's take in the same week.)

takes.why: Take Diggs over Keenan Allen when choosing between the two late veterans.
takes.mechanism: The opportunity with Jayden Daniels is better than the opportunity in Indianapolis.

takes.why: Worth the late shot — the kind of young rookie upside they prefer over aging PPR veterans; ADP already up a round or two.
takes.mechanism: Historic camp buzz (a 27-year Ravens beat writer says he has never seen a rookie camp like it), 6'4/200 third-round profile, and the incumbent WR2 Rashod Bateman is under NFL investigation for a June arrest with a possible six-game suspension — which could force the rookie onto the field earlier than the day-2/day-3 snap base rates suggest. (Name possibly mangled by auto-captions; heard as 'Jacobe Lane'.)
takes.round_or_adp: 'moved up about a round or two'

takes.why: No interest in any way, shape or form after the trade to Houston — he is a waiver-show name later, not a draft pick.
takes.mechanism: He was already inconsistent and touchdown-or-bust while playing a ton of snaps on one of the best passing offenses in football; asking for more from C.J. Stroud on a defense-and-run-game team, arriving this late in the summer, is a downgrade. Xavier Hutchinson may simply start.

takes.why: Not getting nearly enough talk — draft him over the deep rookie fliers.
takes.mechanism: He is second only to A.J. Brown in Drake Maye's training-camp reception counts, on a team that was a top-tier passing-percentage offense last year, and New England has been moving him around into the big-slot role that has historically been very valuable for the Patriots.

takes.why: He deserves to be drafted as insurance, but the ADP spike to the mid-third round is far too high.
takes.mechanism: Elite athletic profile (6'1/220, 4.33) with a day-3 draft slot and no college production — an A.J. Dillon-style combine-over-production profile — on a team you do not expect to score; the spike is being driven by long preseason runs plus the Jeanty injury, and even as a starter he would land in a committee tier with Bhayshul Tuten and Jadarian Price rather than above Rhamondre Stevenson or Tyler Warren. (Rookie name uncertain from auto-captions.)
takes.round_or_adp: 'drafted at like 37 overall' in some post-injury drafts

takes.why: Keep Skattebo at a ninth-round price over Quinshon Judkins at a 16th — all three hosts land on Skattebo.
takes.mechanism: The alternatives on the Giants are Devin Singletary, a bad-preseason Tyrone Tracy and a post-Achilles Najee Harris, so when the team needs to get going three or four weeks in, the workload goes to Skattebo; he is also the better pass catcher, and the unofficial depth chart lists him as the starter with the backup spot unresolved between three names.
takes.round_or_adp: 'keep with my ninth round pick' vs Judkins at a 16th

takes.why: Do not let the name scare you off Skattebo — Najee is not a threat to take the job.
takes.mechanism: This is not the Najee of five years ago (and even then he was not great); he is coming off an Achilles injury.

takes.why: 'A zero-down back' — off the radar.
takes.mechanism: His preseason included letting Jackson Dart get hit and a red-zone fumble the following week.

takes.why: Ranked one spot ahead of Rhamondre Stevenson — trading him for Stevenson is defensible but not an upgrade.
takes.mechanism: They are in the same tier, so the tiebreaker is preference; environment (a better Patriots offense, goal-line work Deshaun Watson has not sniffed in five years) is a legitimate tiebreaker to use, but Stevenson only out-scored Judkins 11.6 to 11.2 points per game last year.

takes.why: Nothing wrong with taking him — back-to-back with Judkins in their rankings.
takes.mechanism: Better offense as the environment tiebreaker, and he was third in Drake Maye's camp reception counts, ahead of Demario Douglas and Hunter Henry.

takes.why: A genuinely underrated Josh Allen stack — but only at the back of the sixth or later; do not force him in the late fifth.
takes.mechanism: He has looked really good in camp after seeming to lose it in Chicago, and he will get ignored in a lot of drafts; the caveat is the opportunity cost at his current late-fifth/early-sixth ADP (Jameson Williams, Luther Burden III, Bhayshul Tuten, Jadarian Price) and the Allen Robinson precedent of great camps that never translate.
takes.round_or_adp: 'late fifth, early sixth round' on Sleeper ADP; 'DJ Moore needs to be back of the sixth'

takes.why: Preferred over DJ Moore as the cheap Josh Allen stack, and a genuine three-outcome swing — take shots like crazy if he makes it to the 10th.
takes.mechanism: He has been great on a per-route-run basis and there is a world where he jumps to the elite tier if the opportunities come — but the same profile has been absolutely worthless year after year, which is exactly why the double-digit-round price is what makes it work.
takes.round_or_adp: 'if Dalton Kincaid makes it to the 10th'; 'double digit round cost'

takes.why: A free stack: if you take Chris Olave and want to wait on QB, take the shot on Shough.
takes.mechanism: Shough is essentially free in drafts, and the Jordyn Tyson injury — though a bummer for the offense — makes the Olave stack cleaner by removing target competition; his starter-pace projection was around 4,200 yards.

takes.why: The anchor of the free Shough stack — clearer target path now.
takes.mechanism: The Jordyn Tyson injury removes the competing target and makes him the unambiguous number one.

takes.why: Jason's favorite stack of the year is Malik Nabers in the third and Dart in the ninth — a true three-outcome player who could fall on his face or win your league.
takes.mechanism: Both players sit at ADPs that do not reflect their good outcomes; the risk is stacked correlation (Nabers coming off the ACL could start slow, Dart is Andy's bust pick under Matt Nagy), so the stack is 'playing with fire' but each leg independently can massively out-produce its price.
takes.round_or_adp: 'Neighbors in the third and Dart in the ninth'; 'waiting for Dart in the ninth'

takes.why: Great value if you get him — but do NOT plan your draft around his third-round ADP; expect him to go in the second, possibly above Drake London.
takes.mechanism: The public ADP is stale, built during the bad-news window on his ACL recovery; now that the news has flipped, every other manager in the room is looking at that same ADP hoping for the steal, so someone reaches. His good outcome does not belong anywhere near that price.
takes.round_or_adp: 'Malik in the third' — but warns he 'will be in the second round', near the A.J. Brown / Drake London / Nico Collins / George Pickens tier

takes.why: A massive value at QB15 ADP in the late tenth — he has never finished anywhere close to that badly, and he is a great consolation prize when Dart goes before you in the ninth.
takes.mechanism: Third-year QB with the fourth-most fantasy points through two seasons ever (QB7 then QB6), led the league in pass attempts, returns all his receivers including a hyped second-year high-draft WR, and then added a star receiver by trade. The only bear case is the first six games (Chiefs, Jaguars, Rams, 49ers, Chargers) — but underdog status is mostly a running-back problem; a QB who has to keep pace in 50-point games is exactly what you want.
takes.round_or_adp: 'drafted at quarterback 15'; 'going in the late tenth'

takes.why: Remains one of their favorite picks in fantasy right now, and the stack partner for the cheap Bo Nix.
takes.mechanism: Same value case as Nix — the Denver passing volume is real and the Nix/Waddle stack costs almost nothing because Nix goes in the late tenth.

takes.why: Borderline undrafted in 1QB leagues — spend your last pick on him, especially if you took Justin Jefferson.
takes.mechanism: Kevin O'Connell's QB resurrection track record (he extracted production from the shell of Carson Wentz and from Max Brosmer), and if Justin Jefferson is the top-3 receiver he has been most of his career, the Jefferson-Kyler stack is the best one in football.
takes.round_or_adp: 'borderline undrafted right now in single quarterback leagues'; 'use your last pick'

takes.why: Yellow flags on his first-round price — all three hosts remain worried — but if he works, the Kyler stack is the league's best.
takes.mechanism: Concern is about where he is being drafted in the first round given the Minnesota QB situation, not his talent.
takes.round_or_adp: 'where he's going in the first round'

takes.why: Capped — not a league-winning outcome, so he does not belong in the high-risk/high-reward bucket.
takes.mechanism: It is established that the pass-catching role now belongs to Kenneth Gainwell.

takes.why: A full three-outcome player — he can be worthless, a flex piece, or win your league if the coaches hand him the job.
takes.mechanism: The upside is real if he takes the job outright; the downside is Seattle's habitual committee behavior — George Holani keeping him off the field the way Zach Charbonnet kept Ken Walker off it.
takes.round_or_adp: named among 'late fifth, early sixth round' Sleeper ADP alternatives

takes.why: Higher ceiling than he is being given credit for, but not a league-winning outcome.
takes.mechanism: If JK Dobbins misses time the work goes to Coleman, not Harvey; and Harvey already caught 47 passes with 5 receiving TDs on his way to RB21, so he would need high-50s/60s receptions to break out from there.

takes.why: The Dobbins pick is getting more nervous by the week.
takes.mechanism: The Coleman drumbeat and hype has reached the point where, if the coaches decide he is the guy, a full transition off Dobbins could happen.

takes.why: Hosts split — Jason says solid-to-great with no bust case, Andy and Mike say he can absolutely bust and also scares them on the league-winning side.
takes.mechanism: The bust case is simply how many mouths there are to feed in Jacksonville; the bull case is that the team's own promotional imagery has him front and center ahead of Trevor Lawrence.

takes.why: The archetype of the three-outcome pick — worthless, flex-worthy, or league-winning if he gets the opportunity.
takes.mechanism: Pure opportunity question: he sits behind the workload, and the range of outcomes is entirely determined by whether the job opens; he also ranks low in Drake Maye's camp reception counts right now (just above Eli Raridon).

takes.why: Availability is the disqualifier; his passing-down work is a plus for Omarion Hampton instead.
takes.mechanism: A mild setback cost him Sunday and Monday practices, and he has an injury history including a lost year in Baltimore — a team wants to use him but cannot keep him on the field.

takes.why: The concentration case — you would love him to absorb the third-down pass-catching work.
takes.mechanism: Keaton Mitchell's inability to stay healthy consolidates the passing-down role.

takes.why: Still the man for the Raiders — the ankle scare is being over-priced, though week 1 is genuinely in doubt.
takes.mechanism: Reporting is a low ankle sprain rather than high, teams are not obligated to disclose the grade, and the market overreacted (his backup went as high as pick 37).

takes.why: The release is the only path forward for a Benson believer — worth monitoring where he lands.
takes.mechanism: He was buried behind James Conner and could not stay healthy; there was no path at all if he stayed in Arizona.

takes.why: Could very well be the starter from day one in Houston despite the Boutte trade.
takes.mechanism: The Boutte acquisition came late in the summer, and reporting suggests the team may not even view Boutte as a starter.

takes.why: 3yr/$45M into the cleanest backfield in football (Pacheco/Hunt gone, only a 5th-round rookie behind him) with goal-line plus new pass-catching role in an Andy Reid offense whose RB1s historically average ~1,400 yards.
Team grooming him as a three-down back (new pass-catching reports), Ekeler gone, only Rachaad White as competition, in what should be a top rushing offense — yet ADP is RB37, lower than last year.
Looked great in preseason; the Packers' two-WR sets are now clearly defined.
takes.mechanism: Preseason usage confirmed Watson and Matthew Golden as the two-WR-set players.

takes.why: 24% overall / 40% red-zone target share with no proven WR competition — a 150+ target ceiling that could break the TE reception record; FF have him firmly TE1 over McBride.
Looked good and is confirmed in the Packers' base two-WR sets.
takes.mechanism: Preseason two-WR-set usage confirmed Golden alongside Christian Watson.

takes.why: Jason has him in almost every draft — the market moved to Burden/Loveland and left Odunze cheaper. Mike is openly anti-Odunze; Sal only confirms full starter participation.
takes.mechanism: He was fantasy WR3 over the first month of 2025 and led the Bears in first-read targets and first-read share under pressure; the collapse dates entirely to the week-9 foot injury, so the hierarchy should reassert under Ben Johnson.

takes.why: Beat reports say ~50/50 rushing split with Kyren Williams in the NFL's #1 yardage offense, projected ~900 total yards, and inherits a top-5 role if Kyren's ankle/foot history flares — round 8-9 price.
McDaniel has led the NFL in pre-snap motion five straight years and McConkey is #6 in YPRR on motion plays; Keenan Allen's 122 targets left; healthy weeks 5-10 he was a top-12 WR — round-4 cost.
Top-12 QB in every healthy season with 400-600 rushing-yard upside, now with Jefferson/Addison/Hockenson under O'Connell — going round 10-11 because of a camp 'battle' he's winning.
May be his own tier at running back, above the rest of the RB1 group.
22.4 ppg in starts with 80%+ snaps (QB2 behind only Allen) with an 800-1,000 rush-yard ceiling; healthy year 3 with Diggs added — near-QB1 upside ~50 picks after Allen.
Cannot be started week 1 in any world; the pick is wasted.
takes.mechanism: Canales explicitly framed week 1 as a committee contingent on Hubbard being healthy, and his RB talk historically trends toward more committee than he first signals.

takes.why: DIRECT CONFLICT: Sal fades hard at RB30/pick 75 (peak hype); Andy is 'very pro Brooks, big time' and says drafting Hubbard now is setting a pick on fire.
takes.mechanism: Sal: Hubbard's hamstring is only week-to-week so the backfield splits on his return, and Brooks is two ACLs deep on a bad offense. FF: Canales said week 1 is a committee IF Hubbard is good to go — a downgrade from 'he's our guy' — and Brooks actually started and played in preseason.

takes.why: Elite talent but re-aggravated a chronic hamstring (now the other one) with a ~2-month timeline and likely PUP; draft only with an IR spot — and it caps Tyler Shough's ceiling.
Jason's official bust pick of the year.
takes.mechanism: Three separable claims: (1) offense/O-line downgrade JAX→NO; (2) 4 TDs on 26 inside-10 carries (15%) and 2 on 12 inside the 5 — a genuine red-zone efficiency flag; (3) 6 receiving TDs on 36 catches is a 3-player, 25-year outlier and 43% of his points came from TDs, so the baseline must regress. Kamara re-absorbs passing-down work by ~week 3.

takes.why: Flatly not draftable right now despite last year's breakout rookie profile.
takes.mechanism: Did not start with the first team and played zero snaps on the first two drives with Herbert, entering only with the backups — because he cannot block, and McDaniel's system requires blocking TEs, which is why they signed Charlie Kolar.

takes.why: Jason leans Rice as a 6th-round keeper over a free last-round Quinshon Judkins.
takes.mechanism: Top-five points-per-game receiver last season whenever on the field, currently going in round 3 — a 6th-round keeper is real surplus.

takes.why: 16.3 ppg on 8.6 targets over his first nine games before hamstring/Baker injuries; Evans' targets gone, and Zac Robinson's scheme made London top-6 — round 4, but track the possible turf toe.
Etienne's ~70% of backfield touches vacated; top-5 in red-zone success rate, elite after contact, taking all first-team reps — round 5-6; FF caveat: LaQuan Allen/Rodriguez committee risk.
Mild caution at a 7th-8th round price — he needs outside snaps in 2-WR sets to justify it.
takes.mechanism: On the starters' only drive he lined up in the slot, and Treylon Burks looks like a real WR3 on a team expected to play heavy 11 personnel. A slot-only role caps the ceiling.

takes.why: Baker's most trusted target with Evans gone and explosion reportedly back — an every-week PPR WR2 going as late as round 13 on some platforms; Egbuka's toe only adds volume.
28% target share (the stickiest stat) with $104M guaranteed and zero credible target competition; TD regression points up, yet priced outside the WR top-12.
All three hosts in: top-10 finish after the midseason OC change, and LaPorta's hip injury frees more targets — worth paying up at current ADP.

Paid like a top TE, reported #1 target without Nabers on the field, Nagy historically feeds TEs — 10th-12th round every-week starter bet; counterpoint (Sal): preseason showed a passing-downs-only 38% snap role.

Vikings rebuilt a vertical wide-zone scheme that fits him exactly (5.86 ypc in outside zone vs Jones' 4.3, 3x explosive-run rate); projects as primary runner and goal-line back at an end-of-draft price.
Payton comps him to Michael Thomas; averaged 6+ targets from week 11 on as a rookie, and preseason usage says he's beaten Troy Franklin for the starting-3 job — late-round or priority watch.
'Undoubtedly Mahomes' favorite target in preseason,' running exclusively with the ones amid Worthy/Thornton injuries — rare late-round rookie who may play 80% of snaps week 1; cut fast if not.
Second-round rookie trending toward a starting role — a live in-season breakout at his round-10 cost.
takes.mechanism: 11 catches, 100+ yards on 13 targets in roughly half a game total, and Christian Kirk (the man ahead of him) has been banged up all camp with no established chemistry with Shanahan or Purdy.

takes.why: 100% of starter snaps in preseason as de facto WR1 on the team with the NFL's most vacated targets (Hill/Waddle gone) — free in every draft; the offense itself is the risk.
Six straight years QB1/QB2 now falling to mid-round-3 in 1QB leagues; finished top-5 two straight years with no top-36 WR, so the opportunity-cost argument dies at this price.
Bottom-5 projected offense; 40% of production was Tua-driven receiving work that Malik Willis won't replicate — workload safe but the double-digit-TD path isn't there at his ADP.

Generational talent drafted near his ceiling on a 3.5-win team favored in zero games, splitting early work with Allgeier/Conner, and nursing a preseason high-ankle sprain; Sal comfortable at round 3 only as an RB2.
Late-season TD burst came without Daniel Jones (8% red-zone target share in Jones games), ankle surgery has no return timeline (likely PUP), compounded by the Keenan Allen signing.
The whole bet is workload monopoly, and new beat reporting undermines it.
takes.mechanism: Houston Chronicle beat writer: the split with Woody Marks 'might not be 50-50 but will be close.' At ~30% for Marks he's fine; at 40-45% he's a big problem.

takes.why: Passed at 1.01: Tua/Penix have looked terrible in preseason and a bottom-five Falcons offense caps him in a way Gibbs never faces.
Great fit on paper; the hosts expect roughly three healthy games — 'the worst fit to go to San Francisco ever.'
takes.mechanism: San Francisco constantly deals with injuries and Evans's own injury history compounds it. (Note: this is a vibes mechanism, not a measured one.)

takes.why: Steelers WR1 'with a bullet' — aDOT collapsed to 10.5 only because nobody worked underneath; Pittman's arrival frees him for the downfield role.
Good real-life fit but the underneath/possession role carries no fantasy upside — never ahead of Metcalf.
70+ catches back-to-back attached to Josh Allen with only 3 games missed; DJ Moore's WR1 status is no lock — stable 11-12 ppg PPR flex floor.

Listed WR2 on the depth chart with weak target competition behind JSN (Kupp 33 and declining, Horton young/banged up); beat reports say 'major factor'. NOTE: Sal also argued the gutted RB room forces pass volume — our check rejects that leg (SEA is a 10.5-win favorite, and leading teams run MORE; vacated carries get absorbed, not converted to passes). Target competition is the load-bearing mechanism, not the backfield.
Former second-rounder buried only by the late Keenan Allen signing; Allen gone, starts 3-wide as top-three target with McConkey undersized and Johnston banged up.
The assumption that he has locked the Cowboys RB2 job is now in doubt.
takes.mechanism: Malik Davis started and played 14 of 31 snaps and left before Blue did — the reverse of last week — turning the job behind Javonte Williams into a three-way battle with Phil Mafah.

takes.why: Extended by the team, multiple top-5 TE weeks late last year vs the same target competition — as likely to hit 50-and-a-TD as the TE7-9 going 3+ rounds earlier.
QB9/3/2/6/8 five straight years, OC upgrade incoming, yet name fatigue has him at his cheapest ADP in five seasons (QB5, round 6 of 1QB).
Jason lumps him with Odunze as a year-three breakout profile he loves.
takes.mechanism: The WR breakout window has shifted: a wave of year-one breakouts caused year-two regressions (McConkey, Brian Thomas Jr.), so the year-three breakout is now the live pattern for high-draft-capital receivers.

takes.why: Mike, a career Swift critic, calls him one of the best picks in the draft — fringe RB1 at an RB24 / round-5 ADP. Treated in-house as a Mike-specific conviction, not a house consensus.
takes.mechanism: The Ben Johnson scheme plus a rebuilt O-line (rush success rate 21st→3rd, yards before contact 26th→6th, PFF run block 14th→3rd) makes his athleticism productive; he is the unambiguous lead, Monangai is hurt, and the Bears are favored in five of their first six games.

takes.why: Sal: 8-of-9 starter snaps (89%) WITH Cole Kmet healthy kills the 'he only broke out on injuries' objection at his TE3/round-4 price. FF: has Loveland and Odunze roughly tied as Bears target co-leaders.
takes.mechanism: Every-down snap share with the healthy incumbent on the field, on a projected top-5 Bears offense — up from a 63% rookie rate.

takes.why: Cheapest true WR1 in fantasy at a round-16 price — a dart you can cut after two weeks.
takes.mechanism: He rested while Bech, Nailor and Benson started with no reported injury — the classic tell that the team already views the role as locked; Jakobi Meyers' targets are gone from the room.

takes.why: Sal: should not be going undrafted at RB50/pick 154 — the clear GB handcuff going behind worse contingent backs. Andy is taking him as the free hedge on his Josh Jacobs fade.
takes.mechanism: 9 of 14 snaps with the starters plus an extra drive with Jacobs out, healthy for the first time in his career; Jacobs was hurt last year, has missed most of camp, and carries suspension risk from off-field legal issues. FF add: Green Bay has shifted toward wide-zone concepts that fit Lloyd, not Jacobs.

takes.why: Andy is not drafting him at all this year; Jason explicitly refuses to fade him and projects 12+ TDs. House is split.
takes.mechanism: His production was a touchdown-machine outcome masking poor between-the-tackles efficiency, and GB's wide-zone shift doesn't fit his style.

takes.why: Sal: roster him everywhere in 14-15+ round leagues — top-20 RB the moment Montgomery misses two games. FF: beat reporting points to a near-even split right now.
takes.mechanism: 100% of backfield snaps on the starters' only drive; a Houston Chronicle beat writer says the Montgomery/Marks split 'might not be 50-50 but will be close.'

takes.why: Appears to have locked the WR3 job with Jayden Daniels.
takes.mechanism: Started opposite McLaurin and Diggs on the starters' lone drive; Washington is expected to run heavy 11 personnel.

takes.why: Roster him in every 14-15 round league as the unambiguous Jets RB2 / Breece Hall handcuff.
takes.mechanism: 100% of backfield snaps and all 4 backfield opportunities with the starters while Hall sat; his 2025 injury was a severe MCL sprain, not an ACL; he is 22, and the only competition (Isaiah Davis) is hurt and a cut candidate.

takes.why: Positive arrow on the Jets' first-rounder but still not draftable in 10-12 team leagues.
takes.mechanism: 60% of first-team snaps this week vs one snap for Isaiah Williams — a full reversal of last week — but he is still the 4th or 5th option behind Garrett Wilson, Breece Hall, Mason Taylor and Kenyon Sadiq.

takes.why: Deep sleeper who could actually matter — a possible Saints WR2 for the first 8-10 weeks. A waiver name, not a draft pick outside 16-20 team leagues.
takes.mechanism: He rested with the starters in the preseason finale after a great camp and rising first-team reps; Jordyn Tyson misses at least two months with a re-injured right hamstring, leaving Olave, then a fading Vele, then Brown. Olave says he reminds him of Rashid Shaheed.

takes.why: Not relevant for 10-12 team leagues yet, but a likely in-season waiver target, especially in the red zone.
takes.mechanism: Played all 8 starter snaps then was pulled after the first drive (a valuation tell); with Malik Nabers still rehabbing an ACL and possibly missing week 1, a 6'5" 218 lb body has a real path past Slayton and Calvin Austin.

takes.why: Live contender for the Cowboys RB2 role, which would be a weekly top-15 RB if Javonte Williams goes down.
takes.mechanism: He started and left the game before Jaydon Blue did, and has shown explosive-play ability when given opportunity.

takes.why: Jason will draft him widely at his late-6th/7th-round cost — the volume finally makes him an easy-button TE1. Mike says Pitts will be on NONE of his teams (mid-round TEs cost RBs/WRs he values more).
takes.mechanism: Kevin Stefanski takes over as HC and has fed the TE 26%+ of team targets in each of his last six years as HC (32% in 2025); Pitts already led the Falcons in routes, targets, receptions and yards while catching from a low-ADOT QB.

takes.why: Jason expects Kamara to be 'a maul' and reclaim the passing-down role by roughly week 3 even if he misses the opener.
takes.mechanism: When he returns he eats the pass-catching work that was the entire source of Etienne's fantasy production.

takes.why: Named the Browns' week-1 starter — which caps the entire Cleveland passing offense. The hosts call the situation worse than Arizona's.
takes.mechanism: His last two Cleveland seasons produced ~62% completions at 6.5 and 5.3 yards per attempt with five fumbles in six/seven games; Shedeur Sanders outperformed him on completion percentage this preseason.

takes.why: CONFLICT: FF calls him the safer Browns pass-catcher to bet on because his value is volume-based; Sal makes him his round-7 refusal.
takes.mechanism: FF: with Watson capping the offense, volume survives where downfield upside gets nerfed. Sal: two new rookies plus other additions competing for targets, on top of the QB situation.

takes.why: Great opportunity, but the upside case dies with Watson under center.
takes.mechanism: Watson's play caps the offense — the downfield/upside profile 'might be nerfed' by the QB situation.

takes.why: The 49ers backup RB job is his by default, but neither host wants to spend a pick — this is a waiver pickup, not a draft pick.
takes.mechanism: Jordan James, the presumed backup, has been injured all camp, so the role fell to him by default rather than by earning it — unlike a clean handcuff situation.

takes.why: Now practicing without a non-contact jersey and looking explosive; the hosts would have picked him in the Dolphins WR debate if he were healthy.
takes.mechanism: He was a borderline first-round talent who fell only because of an ACL injury, and Miami needs someone to step up in a nebulous receiver room.

takes.why: A late-round Falcons rookie getting buzz purely because the target competition is thin.
takes.mechanism: Someone besides Drake London and Kyle Pitts has to catch the ball in Atlanta.

takes.why: Jason has more confidence in Pitts having a season to be proud of than in London delivering a Jefferson-style year.
takes.mechanism: Michael Penix Jr. is gun-shy in the pocket and throws short, which caps a downfield alpha more than it caps a high-volume TE.

takes.why: Total preseason opportunity share — a positive usage signal in a bad offense.
takes.mechanism: Eight of eight backfield opportunities in the preseason game.

takes.why: Andy still took him sixth overall but has now flipped Ja'Marr Chase (and probably JSN) above him.
takes.mechanism: He is not currently practicing and it is a 'weird injury' with vague reporting — double trouble.

takes.why: DIRECT CONFLICT: Sal's worst pick of round 2; Andy traded Omarion Hampton plus more to get him and says he'd have paid more.
takes.mechanism: Sal: a mobile QB in Malik Willis checks down less and steals goal-line/red-zone TDs. Andy states no mechanism — it is stated conviction only.

takes.why: His round-3 refusal.
takes.mechanism: Over the back half of last season Kyren split the backfield nearly 50-50 with Blake Corum, and the Rams kept feeding Corum in the postseason.

takes.why: His round-4 refusal — did everything right as a 1,000-yard rookie, but the offense caps him vs the WRs going in the same range.
takes.mechanism: Bryce Young, possibly in his final year as an NFL starter, will not propel a receiver past better-quarterbacked peers.

takes.why: His round-5 refusal. NOTE: Burrow is a declared untouchable on this roster — this is priced-in noise, not an action item.
takes.mechanism: No mobility, no rushing floor or ceiling, at a price where Jayden Daniels, Lamar Jackson and Jalen Hurts go.

takes.why: Liked him at his round 7-8 summer price, refuses at round 6.
takes.mechanism: Plenty of check-down targets from Rodgers, but he loses red-zone and early-down work to Rico Dowdle.

takes.why: Likes the player, refuses the round-8 price. [CORRECTED 2026-08-25: he is on TAMPA BAY, not PIT — the fade was priced against the wrong backfield; re-read vs the Bucs room where he has locked the pass-catching role.]
takes.mechanism: Elite pass catcher last year (top-5 RB in all receiving categories), but the backfield now has Jaylen Wright on goal line and Boston Scott on early/passing downs.

takes.why: His round-10 refusal — double-digit rounds are for darts, not safe floors. Relevant: Goff is the designated trade chip in DYNASTY TRC.
takes.mechanism: No rushing upside and he will never throw 45 TDs, while Kyler Murray and Malik Willis with real upside go a round or two later.

takes.why: His camp absence was planned rest, not injury — an easy first-round keeper.
takes.mechanism: He returned to practice and the team said time off in camp was always the plan, i.e. they are deliberately preserving him because they intend to give him the ball a ton.

takes.why: Andy would take him over Puka Nacua right now — consistency wins when the elites are volatile.
takes.mechanism: He has been the WR3 basically every year of his career while the other elite receivers have ebbs and flows.

takes.why: Andy's blunt preseason takeaway: 'Ward sucks.'
Drawing targets but catching nothing in preseason.
takes.mechanism: Cam Ward's QB play is the limiting factor.

takes.why: Jason made a trade offer for Waddle immediately after watching the preseason deep connection.
takes.mechanism: His QB's deep-ball skill needed a true field-stretcher and Waddle is exactly that fit — it showed up on tape in preseason. (Note: the hosts named 'Bo Nix' as the QB, which does not match Waddle's team — treat the mechanism as unverified.)

takes.why: The Chargers keep losing offensive linemen — a 'preloaded excuse.'
takes.mechanism: Newly signed center Tyler Biadasz was placed on IR for the season, though Rashawn Slater is back at practice.

takes.why: Mike's my guy at a 4th-round ADP; he believes Loveland finishes overall TE1, past McBride and contending with Bowers. Re-cut 2026-08-28: he names Loveland as the answer to the offseason 'Luther Burden or Rome Odunze?' debate — Loveland is the Bears pass-catcher to own.
takes.mechanism: Closed his rookie year as the centerpiece of the Bears offense (49 targets, four straight double-digit-target games over the final four incl. playoffs), deployed all over the formation rather than in-line, and is the No. 1 option in a Ben Johnson offense whose stated goal is a scoring record.

takes.why: Jason's my guy — drafted at his floor around WR20-22 with top-10 upside.
takes.mechanism: Target share is the stickiest year-over-year WR stat; Wilson averages 28% over four seasons (30% last year) and every other player at 27%+ goes inside the top 12, so the discount is priced off the Jets passing environment, which improves with Geno Smith.

takes.why: Andy's my guy — a rare 'safe rookie WR' worth taking in the 8th despite a 10th-13th-round ADP.
takes.mechanism: 33rd overall draft capital plus a Shanahan offense that game-plans around individual players, a wide-open depth chart (Pearsall out, Kirk hurt, Kittle post-Achilles, Deebo behind Malik Turner) and a record preseason rookie target share — with real traits (6'2" 207, 4.36).

takes.why: Mike's my guy — mid-2nd-round cost for a player he'd take in round 1; overall RB2 upside if healthy.
takes.mechanism: KC signed him to fix a specific deficiency (last in explosive rush rate and forced-missed-tackle rate) that his profile solves (10 runs of 20+, 3rd-best 10+ yard rush rate, No. 1 in forced missed tackle rate), no real depth-chart competition, and Andy Reid's RB1 historically averaged 22 opportunities and ~20 PPR points per game.

takes.why: Jason's my guy — a 7th-round WR29-30 with top-15 upside who can't realistically finish worse than ADP.
takes.mechanism: Top-10 NFL draft picks at WR are effectively guaranteed ~100 targets and near-100% snaps from week one, and Brian Daboll historically funnels enormous volume to his WR1 (Diggs, then Nabers with a similar WR2 and bad QB play).

takes.why: Andy's my guy — a 7th/8th-round QB7 ADP that prices in zero growth; expects a big year-three jump.
takes.mechanism: The main knock (completion %) is one of the lowest-correlating QB stats to next-season PPG while avoided sacks correlates ~3x as strongly and the Bears repaired the line and pressure-to-sack ratio; add rushing upside, three elite weapons, 4th-most end-zone attempts, a 28th-to-9th jump in points per game under Ben Johnson, and the base rate that 60% of first-round QBs top-10 in year two exceed 20 FPPG in year three.

takes.why: Mike's my guy — a late-6th pick he thinks can swing seasons; draft as WR3, finish WR2 or better.
takes.mechanism: His problem was volume, not talent, and volume is now solved by receiver-room consolidation (Doubs and Wicks gone), a new extension, a scheme shift to under-center play action, a move to Z, and an out-route rate jump from 7.7% (2022-24) to 35% — backed by finishing WR11 from week 11 on.

takes.why: Jason's my guy — a three-down back he'd take over Ashton Jeanty.
takes.mechanism: Already owns the goal-line role (80% of goal-line carries) and a pass-catching role with a checkdown QB (19 routes, 3.6 receptions per game as a rookie), the line is far better with Alt and Slater back, Alec Ingold imports the McDaniel outside-zone fullback scheme, and 12 of 15 first-round RBs averaged 18+ opportunities per game in year two.

takes.why: Andy's most locked-in name all offseason — 'this year's JSN' at a round's discount.
takes.mechanism: The sophomore dip was a catch-rate collapse from Herbert under constant pressure plus Keenan Allen soaking targets, not a target decline (only six fewer targets); with Allen gone, a better line, McDaniel moving him around, and no volume threat from Tre' Harris or Quentin Johnston, he is the clear focal point.

takes.why: Andy expects Pitts on many of his teams at a late-6th/7th cost, with PPR value 'through the roof.'
takes.mechanism: Pitts led the Falcons in routes, targets, receptions and receiving yards last season (only McBride matched that) and is now used in a low-aDOT role with 63% of targets under 10 yards, converting volume straight into PPR points.

takes.why: Mike raised Jacobs' risk rating in the UDK; still draftable at the right spot, but if you take him you must bench-stash MarShawn Lloyd.
takes.mechanism: The Packers GM said the team is actively preparing to sustain a possible Jacobs suspension, with wording implying it could land mid-season — an unresolvable variable on a top-three-round pick.

takes.why: A last-round pick and a mandatory bench stash for anyone who drafts Josh Jacobs.
takes.mechanism: A pending Jacobs suspension would open the backfield, and Lloyd's draft capital is barely below Jonathon Brooks' — the market wrote him off purely on injury history with no NFL sample.

takes.why: Jason expects a top-20 PPR week every week in the first month; Andy isn't sure he wants him — consensus is a late-round grab in deeper leagues only.
takes.mechanism: The Colts' pass-catching room is decimated (Pierce and Downs injured, Warren's groin), which is why Indianapolis signed him, so early-season target volume defaults to him.

takes.why: They won't argue him off consensus RB2, but flag that things outside his control can go wrong.
takes.mechanism: The Atlanta team environment: games could be started by Jack Strand or Cooper Rush, and the Penix/Tua situation is a mess.

takes.why: Take Amon-Ra St. Brown over Jeanty in the round 1-2 range.
takes.mechanism: Rounds 1-2 are where you buy reliability and proven production; Jeanty is a projection-type player and those don't belong in that range.

takes.why: Preferred over Jeanty as the early-round pick.
takes.mechanism: Proven, reliable production is the specific asset rounds 1-2 buy, as opposed to projection.

takes.why: Jason would rather take Garrett Wilson in the 4th/5th than London in the 2nd.
takes.mechanism: Both carry the same bad-QB discount but London's isn't priced in — and last year, with equally bad QB play, Garrett Wilson outscored London by about a point per game in shared games.

takes.why: Was a locked my guy most of the offseason and was dropped in the last month.
takes.mechanism: Not enough progress, compounded by his injury situation.

takes.why: Deebo is buried and won't meaningfully cut into Stribling's role.
takes.mechanism: Malik Turner was reportedly taking snaps above him on the WR depth chart.

takes.why: Jason floats him as a quick waiver add if Puka Nacua misses time; Andy and Mike doubt he'd even be the team's top-scoring TE.
takes.mechanism: The Rams have no receiving depth behind Puka (Atwell gone), Ferguson is effectively the WR3 and the team plans heavy three-TE usage — but the room is crowded and he's spent two years learning X/Y/Z.

takes.why: Mike argues Love is being ignored and the Watson consolidation case applies to him too.
takes.mechanism: The pass-rate concern (GB 28th) is offset by elite efficiency among 38 QBs with 200+ dropbacks — 1st in EPA with a clean pocket, 6th in passer rating, 7th in CPOE, 4th in pressure-to-sack ratio — plus a reported shift toward under-center play action.

takes.why: A secondary beneficiary of the Packers thesis, now one of two starters alongside Watson.
takes.mechanism: Receiver-room consolidation after Doubs and Wicks left removed the rotation that suppressed snap counts.

takes.why: Named as another player the Packers consolidation argument applies to.
takes.mechanism: Same consolidation mechanism — fewer bodies rotating through the passing game.

takes.why: They like his role for Jordan Love even though he isn't reliable week to week.
takes.mechanism: Consolidation plus an established slot role, offset by week-to-week volatility.

takes.why: Andy: you're not going to get volume production out of Johnston.
takes.mechanism: The Chargers' passing volume funnels through Ladd McConkey as the focal point.

takes.why: Andy likes him as a downfield piece but says there's no volume production there.
takes.mechanism: Same funnel argument — McConkey absorbs the vacated Keenan Allen volume, leaving a big-play-only role.

takes.why: Mike's answer to 'which Bear do you want' is Loveland, not Odunze or Burden — though a wideout can still pay off.
takes.mechanism: A tight end clears a much lower bar to finish top-three at his position than a WR does, so even if a wideout leads the team in targets, Loveland is the better fantasy bet.

takes.why: Same Bears framing — Loveland over Burden, though Burden could still pay off.
takes.mechanism: Positional bar argument: the TE needs less volume than a WR to return top-three positional value.

takes.why: RB1 overall, arguably his own tier above Bijan Robinson -- take him first without hesitation.
takes.mechanism: Elite offensive environment (Jared Goff, projected top-5-10 scoring offense) with 15+ TD upside and no committee threat (Jamaal Williams gone).

takes.why: Clear RB2 overall behind Gibbs, but the gap is real -- his offensive/QB environment could be bottom-5 in the league.
takes.mechanism: Elite talent and no true committee (Tyler Allgeier gone), but Atlanta's QB situation is genuinely shaky, capping his TD equity relative to Gibbs.

takes.why: First-round pick, top-5-overall upside if he stays healthy -- 24.5 fantasy ppg last year on 400+ touches.
takes.mechanism: Camp tightness report is being handled by the team as precautionary/expected, not a new injury flag; the workload risk is age/wear (30+), not a new data point this offseason.

takes.why: First-round pick, RB4 -- a passing-game floor most people are sleeping on.
takes.mechanism: 3rd in the NFL in routes run (25/gm) and route rate (74%) last year -- no longer a rushing-only back, which raises his weekly floor independent of game script.

takes.why: RB5, first-round pick -- positive receiving-role signal stacked on an existing bell-cow rushing role.
takes.mechanism: OC Pete Carmichael on record wanting Cook to 'bring value in the run and pass game' this year and floated an expanded receiving role week-to-week depending on game plan/matchup.

takes.why: RB6 -- buy the scheme change, not the down year.
takes.mechanism: New OC brings a wide-zone/outside-run scheme Barkley profiles well in, plus an explicit stated plan to increase his role as a pass-catcher; down-year efficiency should bounce back in a scheme built for him. NOTE: the video's coaching staff/system name-check reads as garbled or internally inconsistent (references a 'Sean McVay' system for a coordinator hired away from the Rams/Shanahan tree) -- treat the scheme-fit claim as directionally right but verify the actual OC hire before repeating it as fact.

takes.why: RB7, borderline first-round pick -- literally a top-5 fantasy performer whenever Joe Burrow is healthy.
takes.mechanism: 20 fantasy ppg over multiple different stretches (final 6 games of 2025, 2nd half of 2024) whenever Burrow is under center -- nearly 100 total yards/game, a proven and repeatable QB-health-gated ceiling, not a one-off.

takes.why: RB8 -- should be going early 2nd round, not late 2nd; age regression still hasn't shown up in the tape.
takes.mechanism: Nearly led the NFL in rushing (~1,600 yds, 300+ carries) at 5.2 YPC last year even against stacked boxes (defenses knew Baltimore would run when Lamar Jackson was out); new OC Declan Doyle and a healthy Lamar should only help.

takes.why: Ranked lower than the field has him (RB9) -- receiving volume is the swing risk.
takes.mechanism: Mobile QBs (Malik Willis) tend to keep short-yardage/red-zone touches for themselves on scrambles rather than checking down, which threatens Achane's 67-78 target workload from the last two seasons even though the QB himself is a run threat.

takes.why: Top-10 RB -- clear-cut lead back with both safety and upside.
takes.mechanism: Mike McDaniel's system wants to run; Keon Mitchell is a ~170-lb pure change-of-pace who won't take 10+ touches/game, and Cam'Ron Vidal's extended preseason usage isn't a good sign for him -- leaves Hampton as the clear bell cow behind a ~6-touch complementary role.

takes.why: Still a workhorse-track KC back, but monitor the foot injury before drafting/holding at the top of round 2-3.
takes.mechanism: Camp reports had him becoming a true 3-down back (LT/Westbrook comps volunteered by Andy Reid's staff), but he missed practice this week with a foot injury -- not alarming yet based on current info, but the range of outcomes stays wide until it's clear whether it's a bruise/sprain vs. something more serious like a Lisfranc.

takes.why: Treat the ankle as a real week-1 risk, not noise -- likely misses at least two games even under the more optimistic report.
takes.mechanism: Team language ('more low than high') doesn't square with Schefter's 'not long-term but not good' framing; teams aren't obligated to disclose the grade until week-1 practice reports, and a genuinely low ankle sprain wouldn't need this much hedging -- treat a high-ankle-sprain outcome as live. This nuances the more optimistic Jeanty take already on file (FF, 2026-08-25) toward more caution.

takes.why: Cleanest round-3 red-zone/target profile in the class.
takes.mechanism: Top-5 among RBs in red-zone touches (62) last year plus 51 targets (11th among RBs) in a projected top-3 scoring offense -- one of just 5 backs projected for 10+ TDs this year.

takes.why: Buy the opportunity spike -- should be flying up boards after the Saints backfield got wiped out by injuries.
takes.mechanism: Alvin Kamara (MCL sprain, could miss the start of the season), Devine Ozigbo (hamstring, re-injured) and Ty Chandler (feared season-ending injury in camp) are all hurt, leaving Etienne + Kendre Miller as the presumptive week-1 backfield. NOTE: this directly conflicts with the fantasy-footballers 'official bust pick of the year' take on Etienne already on file (2026-08-24) -- the disagreement is genuine (offense/OL downgrade + TD-rate regression case vs. a fresh opportunity spike) and worth tracking as the backfield news resolves rather than resolving it here.

takes.why: Fine as a forced RB2 in round 3, but not a target -- the timeshare reports keep getting reconfirmed.
takes.mechanism: Reports since May, reaffirmed again in mid-August training camp, consistently describe a 50/50 rushing split with Blake Corum; Kyren keeps the passing-down role but the touch/upside erosion is real even in a great offense.

takes.why: Round-3 dead-zone risk -- health, not talent, is the concern.
takes.mechanism: Missed all of training camp with a groin injury while backup MarShawn Lloyd -- younger, bigger, more explosive -- stayed healthy and looked good; Jacobs isn't getting another 300-touch season after last year's injury history.

takes.why: Talented but a slow-start profile -- won't be startable early even as a top-5 rookie pick.
takes.mechanism: High ankle sprain has cost him essentially all of camp; missing a rookie's install reps is a real cost, and James Conner plus a healthy Tyler Allgeier are both ahead of him to start the year -- expect midseason before he's a weekly factor.

takes.why: Round-5 steal -- should be going 2-3 rounds earlier given the current backfield picture.
takes.mechanism: Best all-around year of his career last year (~1,400 total yards, 10 TDs, top-10 true YPC, top-8 yards/touch at 5.4) even with a bigger workload, and his main backfield competition suffered a hyperextended knee in camp reportedly lingering multiple weeks -- puts him as the lead back in a top-5 offense.

takes.why: Cooled off since the spring -- the backfield got more crowded, not less.
takes.mechanism: Splitting preseason snaps with Tyrone Tracy and Devin Singletary, and the team signed Najee Harris and said he'll be 'a significant contributor' (pass-pro role at minimum) -- this softens (doesn't kill) the earlier all-in FF target take on Skattebo already in the file.

takes.why: No upside, shaky floor -- pass in favor of the WRs going in the same range.
takes.mechanism: Woody Marks has looked great with the 1s in camp and preseason and is reportedly pushing a near-50/50 split; Montgomery's career ceiling (never topped 1,000 rushing yards even in his best years) doesn't clear the bar at his round-4/5-turn cost.

takes.why: Same read as the fantasy-footballers fade already on file -- the pass-catching role is gone.
takes.mechanism: Kenneth Gainwell is the better all-around/pass-catching back in this backfield now, and Sean Tucker (kept over cutting him in free agency) profiles as the red-zone back -- draft the WRs going in the same range instead.

takes.why: Better bet than the reported 'even split' suggests -- he owns the valuable early-down/red-zone role.
takes.mechanism: A recent report calling the backfield 'evenly split' doesn't match usage: Rhamondre gets early downs plus short-yardage/red-zone work while rookie TreVeyon Henderson is limited to obvious passing downs -- the team also didn't trust Henderson with the ball late in the playoffs/Super Bowl.

takes.why: The Steelers RB1 for me -- early-down role plus a real per-touch track record.
takes.mechanism: ~20 fantasy ppg (rushing+receiving) from weeks 5-11 last year once he took over Carolina's backfield, including multiple 200-yard games; new HC Mike McCarthy oversaw his breakout in Dallas and specifically brought him to Pittsburgh.

takes.why: Real receiving role, but don't expect last year's rushing volume to repeat.
takes.mechanism: Coming off a career year (958 rush yds, 333 rec yds, 40 catches) with Aaron Rodgers now back, but Rico Dowdle profiles as the better pure early-down runner -- expect Warren's carries to drop toward 125-150 while he leans on receiving work.

takes.why: Top-30 RB only because he's the incumbent -- not a startable RB1/RB2.
takes.mechanism: Stuck on a bad Titans offense with Tajae Spears already out-snapping him in the first preseason game; ceiling is capped around 12-14 touches at 3.5-4.5 YPC.

takes.why: Talent/opportunity says target; health says hedge -- buy him for value, not certainty.
takes.mechanism: Was top-5 in the NFL in rushing yards/game (77) through 10 weeks last year before injury and would be Denver's clear RB1 in a top-10 offense if he stays on the field, but he hasn't played 13+ games in 5 years, averaging ~6 games started -- the fantasy-footballers' growing Jonah Coleman-nerves take on Dobbins already in the file (2026-08-25) is the other side of this same risk.

takes.why: Priced as a pure handcuff but has a real passing-down path.
takes.mechanism: 1,500-yard season already on his resume (2023) and reunites with a former Arizona State college teammate in Jayden Daniels -- profiles as the Commanders' passing-down back behind the Jacory Croskey-Merritt-led rushing role.

takes.why: One of the better pure receiving backs in the league, now on a new team with real early usage signal.
takes.mechanism: Caught 73 balls last year (with Aaron Rodgers in Pittsburgh, averaging ~15 fantasy ppg in the 2nd half); after a slow start to camp in Tampa, has emerged as the dynamic receiving-down back -- exactly the profile that made him valuable before.

takes.why: Could be a top-30 RB -- the clear-cut backfield-turnover play in Houston.
takes.mechanism: Stood out with the 1s in preseason (all 10 snaps with Stroud when David Montgomery sat, 5 touches for 43 yards + a TD) and reports have him in a near-50/50 split with Montgomery, who has no real ceiling of his own -- Marks is the better pass catcher and could simply take the job.

takes.why: A legitimate top-12 weekly RB if Saquon Barkley ever misses time -- worth a late-round stash.
takes.mechanism: Reasons to expect an increased role even with Barkley healthy: Bigsby himself grades out well, and Barkley just turned 29 with a torn-ACL/ankle-injury history on his resume -- 6-8 touches/game is plausible in the base case, and it spikes hard if Barkley sits.

takes.why: Don't expect him back before November even with optimistic reports.
takes.mechanism: Had ACL surgery in February 2026 -- that's a hard recovery-timeline floor regardless of what a hopeful report says about a week-1 return.

takes.why: Enhancement of the existing Tuten take on file -- the Jacksonville committee roles are now clarified from camp.
takes.mechanism: Camp usage reports describe a specific three-way split: Tuten starts drives (early-down/lead role), LeQuint Allen took third downs before his injury, and Chris Rodriguez works inside the 10/red zone/goal line -- Tuten's lead-back role is real, but the goal-line role (where a lot of RB fantasy points live) may belong to Rodriguez instead.

takes.why: High-variance late-round dart -- off PUP as of this episode, could be nearly free in drafts.
takes.mechanism: Missed camp/PUP recovery plus the Keenan Allen signing has crushed his perceived value, but he's a $100M receiver who's led the league in yards/reception two years running and is a TD threat; his price could collapse to free-agent-wire range purely on name-recognition fatigue, which is the buy signal. Caveat: a brutal opening slate (Ravens, Chiefs, Texans) means he's unlikely to help in the first 2-3 weeks even once healthy.

takes.why: Cheap late-round dart as a real outside-X option on a good offense.
takes.mechanism: Traded to Philadelphia; teammate Saquon Barkley has publicly praised him as a real player, and the hosts project him to start as the outside WR2 alongside Philadelphia's DeVonta Smith/A.J. Brown-vacated volume.

takes.why: A rare 'safe' rookie WR profile per one host -- take him a round ahead of his current ADP.
takes.mechanism: Since 2019, at least 4 rookie WRs have finished top-36 in fantasy every year except one (only 2 last year); this rookie is pitched as the safest bet in that historically-reliable bucket, currently going rounds 10-13 across platforms (ESPN 13th, Sleeper 11th, Yahoo 10th -- call it 10.01).

takes.why: His #1 league-winner at RB — Travis Etienne is gone and over 300 touches from this offense are up for grabs.
takes.mechanism: Etienne's departure vacates 300+ touches; the only competition, Chris Rodriguez, came into camp with a foot injury, offers nothing in the passing game and is not explosive — which is precisely Tuten's entire game.

takes.why: His #1 league-winner at TE — already a top-10 fantasy TE last year and the target competition just thinned out.
takes.mechanism: Ranked 3rd overall in TE targets in 2025 despite his QB getting hurt in Week 13; Michael Pittman's 111 targets are gone, Alec Pierce is coming off March surgery, and Daniel Jones (post-Achilles) will be less mobile and lean on the short-to-intermediate field where Warren operates.

takes.why: His #1 league-winner at QB — mobile-QB upside going as roughly the QB10-11 despite the best situation of his career.
takes.mechanism: Rushing floor plus the best receiving room he has ever had (Justin Jefferson, Jordan Addison, Jauan Jennings, T.J. Hockenson), a good offensive line, and Kevin O'Connell as play-caller — a coach with a record of maximizing veteran quarterbacks.
takes.round_or_adp: going around QB10-11 overall at the position

takes.why: His #1 league-winner at WR — 'feels like cheating' to get him in round 3 (12-team).
takes.mechanism: Led the NFL in red-zone target rate and designed target rate in 2025 and has produced as a top-5 fantasy WR whenever he has played over the last two years; no new target competition arrived (an aging Travis Kelce back, Marquise Brown let go), and the case rests on Mahomes being available Week 1.
takes.round_or_adp: 12-team round 3 = overall picks 25-36 = mid-round 2 in an 18-teamer (MEXICA pick 27)

takes.why: Both hosts are now off him: Jason flipped from refusing to fade to "he's off my board", Andy was already out — the price is only tolerable in the pick-60-75 tier (they'd take Breece Hall, Jadarian Price, Bhayshul Tuten and Bucky Irving over him, and slot him just ahead of Jaylen Warren), and if you draft him you must roster the insurance back.
takes.mechanism: Formally charged with two misdemeanors (battery and criminal damage to property) from the May arrest, court appearance Nov 17; the NFL normally lets the legal process finish first and the Nov 17 date is expected to be a not-guilty plea with trial pushed to Jan/Feb, so the base case is a full 17-game 2026 with any suspension landing in 2027 (~4 games). The live tail risk is the garage surveillance video that produced the charges leaking publicly, which would trigger the commissioner's exempt list immediately — possibly the week he gets you to the fantasy playoffs. Mitigant they flag: no felony charge and the counts are NOT classified as domestic violence, which caps the exposure.
takes.round_or_adp: 12t ~R6, overall picks 60-75 (they say his ADP will fall a couple of rounds)

takes.why: Named as the back who would inherit the Green Bay job outright if Jacobs is suspended — 'that is in fact the starter' — and therefore the mandatory pairing for anyone drafting Jacobs; conviction capped by durability, not role.
takes.mechanism: Jacobs' suspension tail is a knockout risk with no warning, and Lloyd is the depth-2 back; the hosts' own caveat is that betting on Lloyd to play a full game and exit healthy has historically been the wrong bet.

takes.why: Explicit dynasty instruction: 'in dynasty leagues, please make sure Chris Brooks is on a roster' — he is the insurance back to the insurance back in Green Bay.
takes.mechanism: Two-deep contingency: Jacobs carries suspension risk and Lloyd carries injury risk, so the depth-3 back in a bell-cow backfield inherits a real workload in a non-trivial share of outcomes.
takes.round_or_adp: undrafted in redraft; dynasty roster spot

takes.why: Andy's pick as the 2026 Javonte Williams (RB39 ADP -> RB11 finish): an unexciting veteran on a contender, drafted outside the top-24 RBs, who owns the goal line — NOTE this directly contradicts Sal's 2026-08-27 high-conviction fade and our own board's bust-risk flag.
takes.mechanism: Houston converted only ~17% of their attempts inside the five-yard line last year and then went out and acquired a goal-line back, committing to Montgomery in that role; the offense is favored in six of its first seven games before the bye, and whatever Woody Marks does between the twenties, nobody disputes who is on the field near the goal line.

takes.why: Their cleanest 'you'll look back and say duh' pick: a late-drafted rookie RB who looks like he gets everything on the defending Super Bowl champs; Mike drafted him the same day.
takes.mechanism: Kenneth Walker is gone and Seattle's own draft-room footage (Hard Knocks) has the GM calling running back their biggest need; the only competition, George Holani, has roughly 25 career touches and is not pushing a first-round pick off the field. The one hole in the profile — no receiving work in college — is being answered by early camp reports and coach comments putting him in the passing game.

takes.why: A situation worth 100% taking a chance on rather than a settled role: Etienne is out of the way, and the top-12 outcome is genuinely in his range at an RB25 price — the hosts note Jacksonville locked into a single back last year once they picked one, and the same could happen here.
takes.mechanism: Efficiency profile backs the volume bet: last year he converted 5 of 7 carries inside the five into touchdowns, and among 55 qualifying RBs finished 5th in rush success rate, 5th in percentage of yards after contact, and tied for 11th with Breece Hall in forced missed tackle rate. Committee risk is real but bounded — Chris Rodriguez is the goal-line variable and LeQuint Allen the receiving-down variable.

takes.why: Andy's 2026 Trevor Lawrence (QB21 ADP -> QB4 finish): a mobile QB going as the QB17 in the 13th round with a new offensive mind and a real WR1 — Mike pushed back hard, so treat conviction as split, not unanimous.
takes.mechanism: 55% of his 82 career starts have been top-12 QB weeks, and he now gets Kevin O'Connell plus Justin Jefferson after an Arizona scheme that visibly failed to get anyone open; he is also a full year removed from the ACL. Mike's counter, which is the real audit: in his five healthy games last year he averaged 35 rushing yards a game and still never finished as a top-15 QB, and much of that 55% is front-loaded in his early career.

takes.why: Still Andy's answer at the QB22 price, but he explicitly pulled back 'a bit' on the Jordyn Tyson injury — the thesis is a week-6-ish waiver-wire streamer you never give back, especially if Tyson returns in the second half.
takes.mechanism: Over weeks 14-18 last year he completed 70% of his passes, added 27 rushing yards a game and averaged 20 fantasy points per game — a mark Kyler Murray never hit in the same window; among 28 rookie QBs with 100+ attempts in the last five years he ranks 2nd in completion rate, 4th in passing yards per game and 6th in yards per attempt. Kellen Moore raises the play volume, and he did all of it without Tyson, with Chris Olave and Juwan Johnson as the early-season weapons.

takes.why: Jason's pick as the 2026 Trevor Lawrence — the reverse comp, since Lawrence was arguably the 2025 Baker: a disrespected, undervalued QB in a contract year who was already producing before injuries wrecked the season.
takes.mechanism: He was the QB3 in 2024 with 378 rushing yards and ran for MORE last year (382) after everyone said the rushing wouldn't repeat; he was the QB4 through the first six weeks of last season and an MVP candidate before the Evans/his own/offensive-line injuries collapsed the offense. He is not under contract for next season and opens week 1 at Cincinnati with a 51.5 total.

takes.why: Last year's version of this exact screen still hasn't been repriced — 'whenever I look at his ADP I still don't want to draft him, and I should' — the hosts agree he should be going higher than he is.
takes.mechanism: He is the bell-cow back on an offense they like, and everything that produced the RB11 finish (workload monopoly, good offense) is still in place; the discount is a perception lag from his pre-Dallas years, not a change in role.

takes.why: Andy's 2026 Michael Wilson (undrafted -> WR11): a functionally free late-round WR he believes is an every-down player all year, and the late-round shot he is most willing to defend on tape, not just opportunity.
takes.mechanism: He already produced at the end of last year — four top-24 finishes in his final seven games plus 9 catches on 12 targets for 134 yards and a TD in the playoff loss to the Rams — is healthy again, and was rewarded with a three-year extension, which is the team telling you what his role is. Open variable is Tetairoa McMillan moving into the slot, and the QB is still Bryce Young.

takes.why: Mike's end-of-draft pick two days running and an upgrade in conviction from his 2026-08-27 'cheap dart' framing: with A.J. Brown gone he is locked in as the true No. 2 and the beat reporters are raving about the separation.
takes.mechanism: Targets per route run of 23% (2023), 30% (2024) and 21% (2025) — a higher per-route target rate over three years than Zay Flowers, Christian Watson or George Pickens; the historic knock is drops, not usage. The path cleared because the rookie competition faded: Makai Lemon missed heavy camp time and the Stowers hype went backwards.

takes.why: The sexy first-round-pick name in Philadelphia, but the hosts are out this season — 'it will take more time' — and expect Wicks to take the role while he catches up.
takes.mechanism: He missed a large share of camp, and for a player who has never taken an NFL snap those are exactly the reps that cannot be skipped; the hosts describe the Lemon/Stowers hype train as running backwards.

takes.why: Jason's deliberately absurd deep flier ('I recognize this is insane') as the 2026 Michael Wilson — the whole point of the screen is a near-zero-probability profile attached to a player they actually think is good.
takes.mechanism: He went team-by-team looking for a depth chart with no solidified WR1, and Las Vegas was the one: Jalen Nailor isn't good enough and Tre Tucker has flashes but no real emergence, so the room is genuinely open. Beat reporters say Bech has won the starting slot role and he is a better fit in Kubiak's system; the missing ingredient is snaps, which for Michael Wilson only arrived via a Marvin Harrison injury.

takes.why: Considered and rejected as the Raiders' breakout candidate — 'he's just not good enough, we have seen enough of him to know he's not that dude.'
takes.mechanism: Sample-size-is-sufficient argument: he has had enough NFL exposure that continued non-production is treated as a talent read rather than an opportunity read.

takes.why: Also considered and rejected in the same Raiders screen — flashes, but not a player they expect to actually emerge as the WR1.
takes.mechanism: Flash plays without a sustained role; the hosts' framing is that his physical profile caps the workload he'll be given.

takes.why: Passing endorsement: 'what they've done this offseason is to make me like Dontayvion Wicks and Dallas Goedert' — the Eagles' pass-catcher uncertainty concentrates targets on the two proven bodies.
takes.mechanism: A.J. Brown's departure vacates targets and the rookie replacements (Lemon, Stowers) are not camp-ready, so the returning tight end absorbs share by default. Audit note: this is a vacated-target argument, which is the mechanism class that DOES hold — routes must be re-assigned — not the thin-backfield fallacy.

takes.why: Jason bought him in one of his own leagues and still feels good: 'if he's healthy, I don't know how he doesn't score a bunch' — a touchdown-equity bet, not a volume bet, and explicitly NOT a claim on his old statistical level.
takes.mechanism: Red-zone/target-quality reputation on a good offense; the hosts' own framing invokes the 33-year-old-Jerry-Rice comp, i.e. they are pricing decline and betting only on scoring.

takes.why: Take him over Ja'Marr Chase if both are there at the turn.
takes.mechanism: Attached to the reigning MVP in Sean McVay's number-one projected offense, and he outproduced Chase as a fantasy WR last season while Chase just hyperextended his knee.

takes.why: At pick 9 take Lamb, not the RBs who go after him like James Cook.
takes.mechanism: The Cowboys' offense is set up for a repeat of his overall-WR1 season from two years ago.

takes.why: Borderline first-round pick; the ideal round-2 double-RB anchor.
takes.mechanism: Cincinnati added zero backfield competition (Tahj Brooks and a 30-plus-year-old Trayveon Perine), and with Burrow healthy he averaged 20 fantasy points per game and finished top-5 down the stretch for the second straight year.

takes.why: His biggest positive difference in round 2 — a walking top-10 fantasy WR.
takes.mechanism: Drake Maye is the best QB of his career and his target competition downgraded from DeVonta Smith and Dallas Goedert to Romeo Doubs and Hunter Henry after Kayshon Boutte was traded away.

takes.why: Half a round ahead of market; take him over Drake London in round 2.
takes.mechanism: MECHANISM AUDIT: environment-only ('that Dallas offense is hard to ignore'); no usage or role data offered — do not repeat as a reason.

takes.why: A round-2 WR he is buying after camp injuries reshaped the tier.
takes.mechanism: Jayden Higgins' injury removes his main target competition, and newly acquired Kayshon Boutte still needs time to ramp up.

takes.why: Moves up his board and the market hasn't caught up yet.
takes.mechanism: Jordyn Tyson — a rookie with a third straight injury to the same right hamstring — misses at least two months, vacating Saints target share.

takes.why: Fell from a top-15 player to 24th; expect the market to follow him down.
takes.mechanism: An ankle injury whose real status is unknowable until the Wednesday practice report before week 1, because teams file nothing during camp.

takes.why: Borderline top-24 player and still climbing; top-3 WR finish would not be a shock.
takes.mechanism: He has shed the red non-contact jersey and is cutting freely in camp, and his 170-target, 35% target-share rookie year came alongside Wan'Dale Robinson's 140 targets, now vacated.

takes.why: He has never been a Flowers guy and is buying in now.
takes.mechanism: He is the only real target earner left in Declan Doyle's offense — Isaiah Likely is gone, Rashod Bateman has off-field issues, and Ja'Kobi Lane is 'all Twitter hype.'

takes.why: His biggest positive difference in round 3 — a great pick at the 3-4 turn.
takes.mechanism: VERIFIED 8/30 vs Sleeper: Kamara MCL (Questionable, out >=1mo), Ty Chandler on IR, Devin Neal Questionable, Etienne listed depth-chart RB1 — he is the lead back in an offense that leans on RB targets.

takes.why: 'Completely out' — last year was the year to own him, this year isn't.
takes.mechanism: His 126-catch season came from historic garbage-time volume with Marvin Harrison Jr. banged up, and a third-round rookie likely replaces Brissett for six-to-eight weeks including the fantasy playoffs.

takes.why: Only the offense justifies the price; TD upside but not the volume.
takes.mechanism: Camp reports point to a roughly even backfield split with Blake Corum.

takes.why: Amazing pick — a third-round price on a player who usually goes late fourth.
takes.mechanism: Best QB of his career plus zero target competition, on a player who averages 140 targets and 1,000-plus yards whenever he stays healthy.

takes.why: He won't get him in most drafts and is fine with that.
takes.mechanism: A high ankle sprain cost him all of camp and the preseason, and a rookie needing reps must now beat out James Conner and Tyler Allgeier.

takes.why: Do not take him in round 2; take Jayden Daniels four rounds later for similar upside.
takes.mechanism: He outscored Maye, Stafford, Mahomes, Purdy and Lawrence by roughly a point per game or less last year and was not the top scorer over the second half, so a round-2 price buys no positional edge.

takes.why: One of the best RBs available right now — a borderline third-round player going in round 5.
takes.mechanism: Nearly 1,400 total yards and 10 TDs last year while splitting the backfield, and Kyle Monangai's knee injury (Sleeper: Questionable, Knee) may cost him weeks, in a top-three run game under Ben Johnson.

takes.why: Shoo-in for 70-plus catches, 1,000-plus yards and 7-plus TDs at a round 5-6 price.
takes.mechanism: Top-5 in first downs per route run and 13th in yards per route run last season despite the holdout and injury; his only real target competition is an older Stefon Diggs who was slot-only in preseason.

takes.why: Very concerned at a third-round price; he has him as a late fourth.
takes.mechanism: Preseason usage split with Tyrone Tracy, and the Giants signed Najee Harris, who is taking first-team pass-protection reps.

takes.why: Great spot to get him while he is falling in drafts.
takes.mechanism: Back at practice with two-plus weeks of recovery banked and trending to play week 1 (Sleeper wire 8/30: 'looks 100%').

takes.why: Great pick now that injury noise pushed him to round 6.
